title: Organised crime inside the state
summary:
Across the Americas, drug networks have people inside the offices meant to stop them, and most of it is known from courts abroad. In Mexico it reaches whole state governments: in April 2026 a Manhattan indictment charged the sitting governor of Sinaloa and nine officials, among them the mayor of the capital, Culiacan, a senator and police commanders, over protecting a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel; in Tabasco, the state's top police official from 2018 to 2024 is accused of running a cartel-linked gang from his own office. In Venezuela, US prosecutors say the Cartel de los Soles runs through the officer corps; President Nicolas Maduro was charged in 2020, untried, and the former military intelligence chief pleaded guilty in the US in 2025. Honduras has a former president convicted in New York; Haiti has one under US sanctions for financing gangs, which he denies. In Ecuador one decrypted trafficker's phone led to 20 convictions of judges, prosecutors, police commanders and prison officials; in Colombia two former Supreme Court presidents were convicted of taking money to shelve cases against lawmakers tied to paramilitary traffickers.

In south-east Europe the hold runs through prosecutors and judges. In Montenegro, encrypted Sky ECC messages passed on by Europol, the EU police agency, led to charges against the former chief special prosecutor and police commanders over a cocaine clan, and a former Supreme Court president was jailed in 2026 for shielding her son's smuggling ring. Moldova's former governing-party leader got 19 years over the 2014 draining of about $1 billion, 12% of the economy, from three banks. Syria's former ruling family ran captagon pills through an army division.

What the networks buy is protection: raids pointed at rivals, cases shelved, extraditions refused. The map holds 236 cases, proven in 64 countries, including police in Baltimore, Los Angeles and Puerto Rico, where 89 officers were charged in one FBI operation.
implications: Where a network reaches the police command or the prosecutor's office, as in Sinaloa, Tabasco or Montenegro, a resident who reports a trafficker may be reporting to someone on that trafficker's payroll, and cases against the network's rivals move while cases against the network stall. In Ecuador and Colombia it was judges who sold the outcome. Accusations made abroad often change little at home: Venezuela promoted its anti-drug chief Nestor Reverol after a 2015 US indictment, and Honduras's convicted former president has since received a US presidential pardon. Watch who is appointed to run interior ministries, customs and border posts and the courts, and whether officials named by foreign courts are removed or promoted.
uncertain: Several of the largest cases, including those against Maduro and the Sinaloa governor, are indictments that have not been tried, often because the accused stays at home. A US proclamation says Tren de Aragua acts at Maduro's direction, which a declassified April 2025 US intelligence memo doubted, and Colombia rejects the 2025 US designation of President Petro.

title: China's long arm abroad
summary:
In about two dozen countries, from the Pacific islands to Europe and North America, people are doing the Chinese Communist Party's work inside other countries' governments, police forces and elections. The United Front Work Department, a party body that courts Chinese communities abroad and foreign elites, mostly works through go-betweens: community associations, donors, 'friendship' groups and businesspeople.

In Taiwan, Canada, Australia and the United States the route runs through local politics and campaign money. Taiwan's courts are working through cases under its Anti-Infiltration Act, from China-arranged tours that took Chiayi village chiefs to Zhejiang to a small party whose 2022 campaigns prosecutors say were paid for from Fujian; in 2025 four former aides from the Presidential Office and the Foreign Ministry were jailed as spies. In California, Arcadia's mayor Eileen Wang pleaded guilty in 2026 to acting as an illegal agent of China, after her campaign treasurer admitted running her 2022 race on Beijing's orders. Canada's public inquiry found in 2025 that China is the 'most active' foreign interferer there. In Australia a developer who had given about AU$2 million to Labor and over AU$1 million to the Liberals lost his residency on security-service advice.

In the Pacific the route runs through police and money. Uniformed Chinese officers work beside Kiribati's police, a 2022 pact lets the Solomon Islands call in Chinese police and soldiers, and Vanuatu has hosted Chinese police advisers since 2023. A China-funded fund run from the Solomon Islands prime minister's office paid 39 of its 50 MPs. In Europe, Hungary agreed in 2024 to joint patrols with Chinese police, while Ireland and the Netherlands shut Chinese police 'service stations' used to press people wanted by China to go home.

What Beijing gets is votes and posts that favour it, information on governments and militaries, and pressure on its critics abroad. It came to light through security services, inquiries, the rights group Safeguard Defenders and the courts.
implications: For people in these places, a donor, a campaign volunteer or a community leader may be carrying out instructions they cannot see. In Taiwan, village chiefs who take a free trip to Zhejiang come home to voters who do not know who paid for it. In Kiribati and the Solomon Islands, people dealing with their own police may be dealing with officers sent by China. Chinese dissidents in Europe and North America have faced pressure from police offices their host country never licensed. Watch the retrial of former New York governor's aide Linda Sun after her 2025 mistrial, the appeal of William Majcher's acquittal in Canada, appeals in Taiwan's cases, and whether Solomon Islands prime minister Matthew Wale reviews the security pact with China as he promised.
uncertain: Much of this record rests on security-service warnings, expulsions and press reports rather than convictions, and some cases have failed: a Canadian judge acquitted former police officer William Majcher in 2026 (prosecutors have appealed), and Britain dropped its case against parliamentary researcher Christopher Cash in 2025. Reports that China pressed delegations to elect its vice-minister Qu Dongyu as head of the UN's food agency, and Bloomberg's 2018 story of spy chips in servers, which the companies denied, are unproven.

title: Russia's networks in Europe and Africa
summary:
Across a belt of West and Central Africa, Russian soldiers now stand close to the people in power. Africa Corps, the Russian defence ministry's force that took over most of the Wagner Group's African work after Wagner's founder Yevgeny Prigozhin died in 2023, is the only Russian force left in Mali, has its first African base at Loumbila outside Burkina Faso's capital, sits at the air base in Niger's capital that US forces used, and reportedly has up to 200 troops guarding Equatorial Guinea's president, Teodoro Obiang, in power since 1979. Togo signed a defence pact with Russia in November 2025 that lets Russian ships dock at Lomé. Most of these are military governments that sent French or US forces away. In the Central African Republic about 1,000 Wagner fighters have guarded the president since 2018, and a Russian has served as his security adviser. Reporting links some deployments to gold, diamond and timber deals; in Sudan the US sanctioned Prigozhin's gold-mining firm in 2020.

In Europe and the former Soviet countries, Russia works through people already inside politics. Italy's Lega, the party of Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini, still holds a cooperation pact with United Russia, Putin's ruling party, which Il Foglio reported renewed itself to 2027; Austria's Freedom Party had one from 2016 to 2021. In Georgia the US has sanctioned the ruling party's founder for advancing Russia's interests, Belarus voted in a 2022 referendum to allow permanent Russian bases, and in Moldova the governor of Gagauzia was jailed in 2025 for funding a party with undeclared Russian money. Voice of Europe, a Prague news site Czech intelligence exposed in 2024 as Russian-funded, paid European politicians; a former British MEP was jailed in 2025 for bribes from the same circle. Latvia, Estonia and Ukraine are cutting their Orthodox churches off from the Moscow Patriarchate, whose head backs the war.
implications: In Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger and the Central African Republic, the foreign troops guarding the government answer to Moscow, not to voters, and they came in with governments that took power by force; what the host pays them, in cash or mining rights, is not published. In Italy, Germany, Austria and Britain, voters usually learn who paid for a politician's speech only after a raid, a leak or a trial. In Ukraine, Latvia and Estonia, parishes tied to Moscow face new rules. Watch whether the Lega pact ends before 2027, how the German case against the AfD's Petr Bystroň ends, and what Africa Corps receives in Togo and Equatorial Guinea.
uncertain: Links between Russian deployments and gold, diamond and timber deals rest on reporting, not court findings, and troop numbers in Equatorial Guinea and Togo are analysts' estimates. Petr Bystroň is under investigation, not convicted, and Bulgaria's spying case against the pro-Russia leader Nikolay Malinov ended in acquittal in 2026.

title: Governments buying officials in other countries

countries.note: The Chinese Communist Party's United Front Work Department directs 'united front' work among overseas Chinese and foreign elites.

In the 1970s the Korean Central Intelligence Agency and businessman Tongsun Park paid US congressmen ('Koreagate'); the House Fraser subcommittee (1978) also examined the KCIA's use of Sun Myung Moon's organisations.
The Russkiy Mir Foundation (2007) and the Voice of Europe network, sanctioned by the Czech government in March 2024 for paying European politicians.

summary:
Governments are reaching into other countries today in two ways: openly, with soldiers, loans and appointments, and quietly, by paying or recruiting officials. Russia's hand is plainest on its borders. In Belarus, Vladimir Putin promised Alexander Lukashenko a $1.5 billion loan after the disputed 2020 election, and a 2022 referendum allowed permanent Russian bases. In Georgia, the US Treasury sanctioned Bidzina Ivanishvili, the ruling party's founder, who nominates the prime minister, for 'advancing the interests' of Russia. Russia's interior ministry has a cooperation deal with the police of Bosnia's Serb entity and runs a police school in Managua, Nicaragua. Elsewhere the hand is armed. UN experts reported in June 2025 that the M23 group, which took Goma and Bukavu in eastern Congo that year, operates under Rwandan command. UN monitors found 'credible' evidence that the United Arab Emirates armed Sudan's Rapid Support Forces through Chad, and the leader of a UAE-backed movement is a Yemeni vice-president. Uganda sent special forces into Juba in 2025 to protect South Sudan's president.

The quiet kind turns up in inquiries and courts in North America and Europe. In Canada, a 2025 public inquiry said proxies of India's government may still be funding politicians, and a parliamentary committee found some unnamed MPs and senators were 'witting' participants in interference, mostly for China and Russia. In the United States, recent cases have involved Egypt, Venezuela, Cuba, Azerbaijan, Turkey and the UAE; Senator Bob Menendez is in prison as an agent of Egypt, while others ended in a pardon, a dismissal or an acquittal. In Israel, two aides of the prime minister were arrested in 2025 on suspicion of taking money to promote Qatar. France holds formal power in two small neighbours: its president is co-prince of Andorra, and Monaco's prince consults Paris before naming his head of government. In the 1970s South Korea's intelligence agency had a businessman pay 30 US congressmen.
uncertain: The Canadian inquiry wrote that India's proxies 'may' have given money, and the parliamentarians the committee described have never been named. A US sanction on Ivanishvili and arrests in Israel are not verdicts, and several US cases ended without a conviction.

implications: In eastern Congo, people in Goma and Bukavu live under an administration the UN says answers to another country's army. In Georgia, the man who chooses the prime minister is under US sanctions for serving Russia. In Canada and the United States, voters cannot tell which donations or community groups are fronts, and cases that do reach court often end without a verdict. What has made this visible is registration: Australia (2018), the UK (2023) and Canada (2024) now require people acting for foreign states to register. Watch for consulting contracts with foreign state companies, sudden clusters of donations, officials pushing one country's line on arms or sanctions, and how the open cases in Israel, Canada and Brussels end.

title: Governments inside companies
summary:
Several governments sit inside companies today, some openly by law and some through spies; China does both. Its company law requires a Communist Party organisation in any firm with three or more party members, and the party reported in 2018 that 73.1% of private companies had one; ByteDance, owner of TikTok, has had a party committee since 2014 and, since 2021, a state fund on the board of its main Chinese subsidiary. Abroad, Salt Typhoon, a hacking group widely attributed to China's Ministry of State Security, sat inside at least nine US telecom carriers, including Verizon and AT&T, with access to call records and wiretap systems, and three Germans are on trial accused of gathering naval technology for that ministry through a private firm.

Russia, Iran, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia take companies at home. In 2023 Russia's state property agency took over Danone's Russian business and Carlsberg's Baltika brewery, and a nephew of Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov came to run Danone Russia. Iran's Revolutionary Guards, its ideological military force, control more than 812 companies through their engineering arm Khatam al-Anbiya, and Guards-linked foundations bought control of the national telecom company in 2009. Turkiye's trustee fund held 1,056 businesses by October 2025 after seizing those it called Gülen-linked, and Saudi Arabia's 2017 Ritz-Carlton detentions ended in settlements with 87 business people and princes.

North Korea works through payrolls. Its programmers take remote jobs under stolen identities and send the wages to its weapons programmes; one Arizona laptop farm put them into more than 300 US companies and a New Jersey scheme into more than 100, and in 2025 Google found them seeking work in Germany, Portugal and Britain. Its hackers took about $1.5 billion from the Dubai exchange Bybit. Some governments push back: Italy used its national-security powers to limit Chinese state owner Sinochem's control of Pirelli. Most of it came out through prosecutions, leaks and security reports.
implications: A phone customer in the United States, a TikTok user, a Danone shareholder or an employer hiring a remote developer usually cannot tell whether a party committee, a foreign spy service or a state trustee sits inside the firm. Where companies are seized, as in Russia and Turkiye, owners lose them without a court verdict and staff answer to new political managers. Where software or telecom suppliers are breached, one break-in reaches thousands of customers, as when SolarWinds' poisoned update went to about 18,000. Watch for further 'temporary management' seizures of foreign-owned firms, remote hires whose identity cannot be checked, and foreign state stakes in grids and telecoms, such as State Grid of China's 40% of the Philippine power grid.
uncertain: US officials say Kaspersky gives Russia's FSB access, which the company denies, and Philippine senators' worries about Chinese control of the national grid have not been shown to involve misuse. German investigators say Wirecard's former COO Jan Marsalek worked with Russian intelligence; he has not been tried.

title: Foreign money inside Europe's parliaments
summary:
Several foreign governments have found members of Europe's parliaments willing to speak and vote for them for money, and courts in Belgium, Germany and Britain are still dealing with it. The European Parliament in Brussels, the EU's elected assembly that votes on laws and budgets for 27 countries, is at the centre. Belgian prosecutors say Qatar and Morocco paid members to favour them, much of it through Fight Impunity, a Brussels human-rights charity run by a former MEP; police found bags of cash at the home of Greek MEP Eva Kaili, then one of the Parliament's 14 vice-presidents, who is charged and denies it. A second Belgian case alleges gifts, travel and football tickets from the Chinese telecoms firm Huawei to MEPs from Italy, Bulgaria and Malta.

Russian money has reached members from Britain, Germany, Hungary and Latvia. A former UK MEP is in prison for taking bribes to make pro-Russian statements, a Hungarian MEP was convicted of spying for Russia, leaked emails showed a Latvian MEP reporting to officers of Russia's FSB security service since at least 2004, and German prosecutors are investigating an AfD politician over cash from Voice of Europe, a Prague news site Czech intelligence exposed as Russian-funded.

Azerbaijan showed the method. The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) gathers MPs from 46 national parliaments and reports on elections and political prisoners. About $2.9 billion moved through Danske Bank's Estonian branch in 2012–2014, some of it reaching people who defended Azerbaijan there; an Italian former group leader was jailed for taking €2.39 million, and Germany's parliament lifted two members' immunity.

Beyond the EU, in Israel two of Prime Minister Netanyahu's aides are suspected of taking money through a US lobbying firm to promote Qatar, and in Georgia the US sanctioned the ruling party's founder for advancing Russia's interests. Most of it surfaced through police raids, leaked bank records and intelligence briefings.
implications: Voters see the speech or the vote; they do not see the payment made through a charity, a shell company or cash handed over at a meeting. When members are paid to defend Azerbaijan in PACE, what is being bought is the assembly's verdict on Azerbaijan's elections and political prisoners, and the prisoners are the ones who lose. Those caught come from centre-right, socialist and nationalist parties alike, and the paying states include Qatar, Morocco, Azerbaijan, Russia and China. Watch the Qatargate and Huawei trials in Belgium, the Bystroň inquiry in Germany, the Israeli investigation of Netanyahu's aides, and whether parliaments tighten their rules on charities, gifts and side income.
uncertain: Eva Kaili, the Huawei suspects and Petr Bystroň are charged or under investigation, not convicted, and they deny wrongdoing. The US sanction on Georgia's Bidzina Ivanishvili is one government's judgement, not a court finding.

title: Turkey's long arm: chasing the Gülen movement
roles: Country that handed people over or closed schools
summary:
Turkey's government is still reaching into other countries for people it links to the Gülen movement, a religious network built by the preacher Fethullah Gülen that ran schools and charities in many countries. Turkey calls it a terrorist group, 'FETÖ', and blames it for the failed coup of July 2016. At home that blame emptied whole parts of the state: the day after the coup 2,745 judges, about a third of the bench, were removed, and about 23,000 police, 15,000 military personnel and some 150,000 public employees in all followed.

Abroad the reach runs along three lines. Across Africa and South Asia, governments handed Gülen-linked schools to Turkey's state Maarif Foundation: Senegal, Chad, Niger, Guinea, Somalia and Sudan did so in 2017, Senegal's schools alone teaching about 3,000 children, and Pakistan's Supreme Court ordered the same in 2018. Turkmenistan jailed 18 men in closed trials; Kazakhstan refused, and its 33 lyceums were renamed. In Kenya, Kosovo, Moldova and Malaysia, people themselves were taken: Kosovo flew five teachers and a doctor to Turkey in 2018, Moldova's intelligence service sent seven teachers, and in October 2024 Kenya returned four Turkish refugees 'at the request of the government of Türkiye'. In Germany, Austria and Belgium the line runs through mosques. The Diyanet, Turkey's state religious office, employs imams abroad as civil servants and gave Turkey's parliament reports on Gülen followers in 38 countries; German prosecutors have investigated imams of its German branch, DITIB, for spying.

Some have pushed back. Kosovo jailed its intelligence chief over the deportations, the European Court of Human Rights ruled against Moldova's transfers, and Interpol refused 773 Turkish wanted-notice requests as political. The movement worked on foreign governments too: groups tied to it paid for about 200 trips to Turkey for US members of Congress and their staff.
implications: For a Turkish teacher, refugee or school owner living in Nairobi, Chișinău or Pristina, legal residence has not been a guarantee: host governments have detained people and flown them out within days, without a public hearing. Families in Dakar, N'Djamena and Niamey found their children's schools under new Turkish state management. Inside Turkey, thousands of judges and police officers were replaced at once, so cases are now heard and investigated by people appointed after the purge. Watch for further handovers from countries that host Turkish refugees, court rulings against them, and how Germany, Austria and Belgium treat imams employed by Turkey's state.
uncertain: Turkish courts treat the 2016 coup as a Gülen operation and the movement denies it; many of those removed were dismissed by decree rather than after an individual trial. The German inquiry into DITIB imams is recorded here as an investigation, not a verdict.

title: Churches and movements placing members in the state
summary:
Members of religious movements hold some of the highest offices on Earth today, while in a few countries the state is breaking such movements up. Japan shows both at once. The Tokyo High Court upheld the dissolution of the Unification Church, a Korean-founded church, in March 2026 after a lower court found 1,559 victims of its donation drives. The ruling Liberal Democratic Party's own 2022 survey found 179 of its 379 lawmakers had dealings with the church. At the same time Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, chosen in 2025, sits in the Diet league of Nippon Kaigi, a nationalist lobby, along with 10 of her 19 ministers, while 12 belong to the league of the Shinto shrines' political arm. In South Korea a court jailed the Unification Church's leader in August 2026, and the founder of another church, Shincheonji, was indicted after at least 56,472 followers were signed up to the governing party.

Elsewhere the placement is open and lawful. India's prime minister Narendra Modi was a full-time organiser for the RSS, the Hindu nationalist volunteer body; in 2020, 38 of 53 BJP ministers had RSS roots. In Latin America, Chile's president José Antonio Kast was raised in the Catholic Schoenstatt movement and his under-secretary of justice is a celibate member of Opus Dei; Ecuador's president from 2021 to 2023 was reported as a married Opus Dei member; and in Brazil an evangelical caucus votes as a bloc in Congress. Indonesia's vice-president from 2019 had led Nahdlatul Ulama, its largest Muslim organisation, and Ethiopia's prime minister preaches at a Pentecostal church.

Turkey runs the other way. After the 2016 coup attempt it blamed the Gülen movement, an Islamic network that had placed graduates of its schools in the police and courts, dismissed about 150,000 public employees, including 2,745 judges in a single day. In all, 40 countries show members in government and 16 have banned or purged a movement.
uncertain: Membership in most of these movements is reported by the press and the movements themselves do not publish rolls; Opus Dei has said William Barr is not a member, and the PAN denies Mexico's El Yunque had a role in it. The figure of 290 church-backed LDP candidates in 2021 comes from church documents reported in the press, not from a court.

In Japan, the families who gave money to the Unification Church watched it keep close ties to lawmakers for decades. In Turkey, tens of thousands of police, soldiers and judges lost their jobs on the basis of alleged membership. Watch for mass party sign-ups, bloc endorsements, church volunteers in campaigns, and dismissals justified by membership alone.

title: Religious nationalism in power
summary:
In several Asian countries today, the people who run the government and the people who run a religious-nationalist movement are largely the same. In India the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), a Hindu nationalist volunteer group founded in 1925, is the parent of the ruling BJP. Prime Minister Narendra Modi was a full-time RSS organiser before it lent him to the party in 1985, the vice president has been with it since age 16, and in 2020 the news site ThePrint counted RSS roots in 38 of the 53 BJP ministers. In Japan the Diet leagues of Nippon Kaigi, a nationalist lobby of about 40,000 members that campaigns to revise the post-war constitution, and of the Shinto Political League, the political arm of the shrine association, take in most of the cabinet: 10 and 12 of Sanae Takaichi's 19 ministers in October 2025, by the Communist Party paper's count, and 15 and 16 of 19 under Shinzo Abe in 2014.

In Sri Lanka and Myanmar, Buddhist nationalist monks reach the state through favours rather than seats. Myanmar's four 2015 laws on conversion, marriage and birth spacing came from texts proposed by the monks' group Ma Ba Tha, and the military government dropped sedition charges against the anti-Muslim preacher Wirathu and gave him a top honour in 2022. In Sri Lanka the defence secretary opened the Bodu Bala Sena's training centre in 2013, and as president he put its leader Gnanasara in charge of a legal-reform task force in 2021; the Supreme Court voided his 2019 pardon in September 2026.

Hizb ut-Tahrir, which wants a single worldwide caliphate, works from outside by recruiting officers. Pakistan's army convicted a brigadier and four majors in 2012, Bangladesh's army named it in a coup plot that year, and Indonesia (2017) and Britain (2024) banned it.
implications: Membership of these movements is lawful, and their members win elections. What changes is that a movement's aims can become government policy without a public argument about the movement: constitutional revision in Japan, a single legal code in Sri Lanka, limits on conversion and interfaith marriage in Myanmar. Religious minorities feel it first, as Muslims in Myanmar and Sri Lanka did when preachers accused of stirring violence against them were honoured or given official posts. Watch who sits on cabinet committees and who drafts laws on religion and family, and whether courts can still undo political favours, as Sri Lanka's did in 2026.
uncertain: The Japanese cabinet counts come from the Communist Party's paper and press reports of Diet league lists, and the Indian figures from journalists, since the RSS keeps no published membership roll. Being in a Diet league does not show how much a minister follows the lobby's aims.

title: Governments that export religion
roles: Where the mosques or churches are
summary:
Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Russia run or pay for mosques and churches abroad, and host countries from the Baltic states to Belgium and Austria are now cutting those ties. Turkey's Diyanet is the state religious directorate: it employs imams as civil servants and runs over 2,000 mosques abroad, through branches such as DITIB, one of Germany's largest Muslim organisations, and ATIB in Austria. Saudi Arabia worked through the Muslim World League, and donors from four Gulf states funded Dutch mosques. Russia works through the Russian Orthodox Church (Moscow Patriarchate), whose head, Patriarch Kirill, backs the war in Ukraine.

The break is sharpest along Russia's western border. Latvia made its Orthodox Church independent of any church authority outside the country in 2022. Estonia sent home the Moscow Patriarchate's metropolitan in 2024, and tightened its churches law. Ukraine banned the Russian church in August 2024 and gave affiliated bodies nine months to cut ties. Britain, Canada and Ukraine have sanctioned Kirill.

Further west the dispute is over who picks imams and what they report home. After Turkey's failed coup in 2016 the Diyanet told its imams abroad to gather information on followers of the Gülen movement and handed Turkey's parliament reports from 38 countries. Germany cut DITIB's federal funding in 2018, and Austria, which bans foreign funding of religious bodies, put about 40 ATIB imams' residence permits under review. Belgium took the Great Mosque of Brussels back from Saudi control in 2018, 51 years into a rent-free lease, then blocked a new board in 2020 when its security service found members tied to Moroccan intelligence and to the Diyanet. A Dutch inquiry in 2020 found Gulf money shaping the choice of imams.

The sponsoring state gets a say over what is preached to its people abroad, and in Turkey's case names of its opponents. Most of it came out through parliamentary inquiries, security services and Turkey's own reports to its parliament.
implications: For a congregation, it is often hard to tell where the money and the instructions come from. Diyanet imams abroad were told to report on Gülen followers in their own mosques, and those reports went to Turkey's parliament. Orthodox believers in Ukraine, Latvia and Estonia now find the question of which church their parish belongs to settled by law. Host governments use funding bans, residence permits and church laws, and the sponsoring state may call that an attack on religion, as Turkey did in Austria. Watch how Ukraine applies its ban to individual parishes, whether any Orthodox church recognises Latvia's independent church, and how host states pay imams once foreign money is cut off.
uncertain: A German court said spying by DITIB imams could not be proved, so that part of the Turkish case is unproven. Kirill's description as a KGB agent comes from Swiss police files, not a court, and an EU sanction on him was dropped when Hungary objected.

title: Consultants and lobbyists inside the ministries
summary:
Inside many governments today, some of the people shaping policy are on loan from private firms. The Tony Blair Institute for Global Change, a London non-profit, reports advisers in more than 45 governments and about 1,000 staff; in Rwanda it helps run strategy and delivery units in the president's and prime minister's offices, and its largest donor is Larry Ellison's foundation. In Britain the Big Four accounting firms, Deloitte, EY, KPMG and PwC, lend staff to the Treasury to help write tax law, and a parliamentary committee found they can then advise clients on it; in Australia a PwC partner advising the Treasury shared its confidential tax plans with at least 53 PwC partners. In France a Senate inquiry called the state's use of consultants 'sprawling and opaque', and prosecutors seized €65 million in 2026 in a tax-fraud inquiry into McKinsey, a US consulting firm.

South Africa shows how far this can go. The Zondo Commission into state capture found that President Jacob Zuma, his tax chief and Bain & Company together took over the revenue service, SARS, partly to stop it investigating corruption. McKinsey admitted to the US Justice Department in 2024 that it conspired to bribe officials at Eskom and Transnet, the state power and rail companies, and paid $122 million. KPMG withdrew a report that had fed charges against a former finance minister, and the London PR firm Bell Pottinger ran fake online accounts defending the president's circle.

In Europe and North America, companies reach the top by phone and text. Leaked Uber files show economy minister Emmanuel Macron helping the company in France and a former EU commissioner lobbying Dutch officials. David Cameron texted Britain's chancellor for Greensill Capital. Ursula von der Leyen negotiated the EU's largest vaccine contract partly by text with Pfizer's chief, and Canada's ethics commissioner found Justin Trudeau broke conflict law over SNC-Lavalin, an engineering firm facing bribery charges.
implications: When a firm helps write a tax law in London or Canberra, the same firm can then sell its clients advice on that law, and the public cannot see where one job ends and the other begins. In South Africa the tax service was restructured in a way the Zondo Commission found was partly meant to stop it investigating corruption. Contracts, texts and seminar notes are rarely published, so the record arrives years later through inquiries, leaks and court cases, and penalised firms keep working: Britain lifted its ban on Bain two years early. Watch which outside advisers sit in your government's central offices, who pays them, and whether ministers' messages with companies are kept.
uncertain: Bain denies it wilfully helped capture SARS, and inquiries found David Cameron broke no lobbying rules. The Uber Files show what Uber staff wrote about officials, and the account of Neelie Kroes's lobbying rests on those documents alone.

title: Global firms buying governments
summary:
Across Latin America, southern Africa and parts of Asia, the courts are still working through what a few global firms paid the people who run governments. The largest web runs from Brazil. Odebrecht, a construction group, admitted in 2016 to paying $788 million in bribes in a dozen countries through a department set up for the purpose. The trail runs through Peru, where two former presidents are serving 20 and 15 years; Ecuador, where a vice-president was jailed; the Dominican Republic, where a public works minister was convicted over $92 million; Panama, where a money-laundering trial opened in 2026 with former president Ricardo Martinelli taking part by video from asylum; and Mexico, where a former head of the state oil company Pemex is accused of taking $10 million.

Swiss commodity traders, which buy oil and metals from state companies, have admitted the same. Glencore pleaded guilty to bribery in Nigeria and four other African states and agreed to pay over $1 billion, plus $180 million to Congo; Gunvor was convicted over Ecuador and Trafigura pleaded guilty over officials at Brazil's Petrobras. In Mozambique, about $2 billion in loans for a shipbuilder's projects were partly hidden from the IMF, and a former finance minister was convicted in Brooklyn. Malaysia's former prime minister Najib Razak was convicted over money from the 1MDB fund whose bond deals Goldman Sachs bankers arranged, and in New York Gautam Adani faces charges, which he denies, of paying Indian officials over $250 million.

The same trade works inside rich countries. In Illinois and Ohio, power companies bought support for their bills from House Speakers; Ohio's paid about $60 million to win a $1 billion-plus rescue of its nuclear plants. In South Africa, an inquiry found ministers and state-company heads acted corruptly for the Gupta family. Firms run by Erik Prince, Blackwater's founder, now sell security to Haiti, Ecuador and Congo.
implications: The bribe is built into the price of the highway, the oil cargo or the power contract, so people in Peru, Nigeria or Ohio pay it through tolls, lost oil income and electricity bills. In Mozambique, hidden loans added about $2 billion to a debt the public had never been told about. Laws can follow the money, as Ohio's nuclear rescue did. Few of these cases began in the country where officials took the money. Watch Najib's and Trafigura's appeals, the Adani case, the Panama trial, the long-running charges against Emilio Lozoya in Mexico, and how far Prince's firms go in policing and tax collection in Haiti.
uncertain: Brazil's Supreme Court annulled Lula da Silva's convictions in 2021, so he is not a convicted Odebrecht case. Adani and Lozoya are charged, not convicted, and the claim that Odebrecht gave $35 million to Nicolás Maduro's 2013 campaign rests on one executive's statement.

title: Industries inside their regulators
summary:
In many places today, the companies a public body oversees have people inside it or help write its rules. At the UN climate talks, oil states hosting the summit put oil executives in charge: COP28 in Dubai in 2023 was led by the chief executive of ADNOC, the UAE state oil company, whose leaked briefing papers included oil and gas talking points, and COP29's chief executive in Azerbaijan was filmed discussing oil and gas deals. In the United States, Boeing staff carry out much of the safety certification the Federal Aviation Administration is meant to do; in statehouses, reporters found at least 10,000 bills from 2010 to 2018 copied almost word for word from model legislation, more than 2,100 of which became law; and in Ohio, FirstEnergy channelled about $60 million to the House Speaker's circle for a $1 billion-plus rescue of its nuclear plants.

In South Africa, foreign firms admitted to US prosecutors that they bribed officials at the state power and rail companies and in Johannesburg and Tshwane: McKinsey paid $122 million and SAP more than $220 million. In Latin America the Brazilian builder Odebrecht admitted $788 million in bribes in a dozen countries; Peru has sentenced a former president to 20 years, and Panama's trial opened in January 2026. In Brazil's Congress, the farm caucus's agenda is drafted by a think tank funded by 48 business groups whose members include Bayer, BASF and Cargill. In Europe, Belgian prosecutors are investigating alleged payments by Huawei associates to members of the European Parliament, and Ukraine's anti-corruption bureau says a businessman close to President Zelensky ran a $100 million kickback scheme at the state nuclear company.

What the industries get is rules, safety checks and contracts shaped before the public knows a decision is being made. Most of it came out through leaks, lawsuits, inquiries and foreign prosecutions.
implications: For passengers, patients and tenants this is a safety question as much as a money one. Grenfell's cladding passed British fire certification on a false basis, and 72 people died; France's drug regulator was fined for failing to act on Servier's Mediator; a Japanese parliamentary inquiry found the nuclear regulator had been captured by TEPCO before Fukushima. Voters usually cannot see who drafted a bill or ran a safety test. Watch company staff doing a regulator's checks, officials moving between a regulator and the industry it oversees, identical bills in many legislatures, and industry delegates at UN talks on climate, shipping and tobacco.
uncertain: Sultan Al Jaber called the COP28 claims false; the Huawei, Energoatom and Panama cases are allegations or trials not yet decided. A Senate minority staff memo counted $2.37 billion in regulatory liabilities facing Elon Musk's companies during his time at DOGE, but no wrongdoing has been found. John Perkins's 'economic hit man' account of inflated forecasts rests on his own book.

title: Criminal money inside banks and firms
summary:
In more than fifty countries, criminal groups own banks and companies or work from inside them. In Brazil the PCC, the country's largest criminal organisation, is accused of owning two São Paulo bus companies, one running about 1,200 buses, and of holding about 30 billion reais through some forty investment funds: four ethanol plants, a port terminal, about 1,600 trucks and more than a thousand petrol stations across ten states. In Mexico the US in 2026 named CJNG cartel firms in agave, tequila and fuel retail, and naval officers and customs officials were arrested over fuel imported under a false label through ports the navy runs. In Cambodia scam compounds sit inside big business groups; in 2026 the US designated a sitting senator's network and added 26 entities to its Prince Group listing.

At Europe's big container ports, Antwerp and Rotterdam, cocaine crews recruit terminal staff and IT contractors who hand over release codes; over 1,826 tonnes of drugs were seized in or bound for EU ports in 2019–2024. In Italy the Calabrian mafia, the 'Ndrangheta, ran building firms in Emilia-Romagna, including in rebuilding after the 2012 earthquake.

Much of it moves through ordinary banks. Wachovia took some $378 billion from Mexican exchange houses; HSBC paid $1.9 billion over Sinaloa cartel cash; Danske Bank's Estonian branch moved about 200 billion euros of non-resident money; Credit Suisse became the first major Swiss bank convicted of a crime. In Honduras the US named a bank owned by a former vice-president's family as a traffickers' laundering channel. Newer rails carry the same money: darknet markets, bitcoin mixers, exchanges such as Binance, which paid $4.3 billion in penalties, and encrypted phone networks, whose hacked messages underpin hundreds of European prosecutions.

What the groups get is a legitimate invoice, a payroll and sometimes a contract with the state. It comes to light through prosecutors, US Treasury designations and police who break into their networks.
implications: A bus passenger in São Paulo, a driver filling up at one of those petrol stations, or a depositor at a Honduran bank uses a business that looks normal and may be carrying criminal money. Port workers in Antwerp and Rotterdam are the people the crews try to recruit. The usual outcome for a bank is a fine paid by the company with no individual charged, as with HSBC, so the same channel can reopen under new names, as the Baltic banks did after Danske. Watch for designations against firms with public contracts, ports and free zones where staff are arrested, and settlements in which nobody is named.
uncertain: Many of the Brazilian and Mexican cases are charges or investigations, not verdicts. Panama's court acquitted the Mossack Fonseca founders of money laundering in 2024, and the pictures of drug production in Syria's Sweida and of gold leaving the Central African Republic rest on estimates and reports rather than court findings.

title: Companies inside other companies
summary:
In the chip, telecom and port industries, governments are now fighting over firms that a rival company, often one answering to a foreign state, has reached inside. In the Netherlands the chipmaker Nexperia belongs to Wingtech, a Shanghai firm with almost 30% of its shares tracing back to the Chinese state; in October 2025 the Dutch economy ministry took over Nexperia's governance, China blocked exports of its chips, and European carmakers ran short. A Dutch court has since ordered an investigation into mismanagement. In northern Australia the Port of Darwin, near a base used by US Marines, is leased for 99 years to Landbridge, whose owner has close ties to the Chinese Communist Party; both main parties promise to take it back, and Landbridge has begun arbitration to stop a forced sale. In a Brooklyn courtroom Huawei, China's largest telecom-equipment maker, is on trial on charges of stealing secrets from five US companies over about 20 years. Under China's 2017 National Intelligence Law, Chinese organisations must help state intelligence when asked.

Across East Asia the way in runs through engineers. Taiwan sentenced a former TSMC employee in 2026 to 10 years for passing 2-nanometre chip secrets to help Tokyo Electron. In South Korea a former Samsung executive is charged with copying a Samsung chip factory in China with about $340 million from the Chengdu city government. Micron's memory designs moved through Taiwan's UMC, which pleaded guilty in the US.

In state-owned companies elsewhere, the way in runs through bribes to managers. ABB paid more than $37 million to an official at Eskom, South Africa's power utility; Ericsson paid officials at Djibouti Telecom; a Vitol oil trader was convicted of bribing officials at Mexico's Pemex and Ecuador's Petroecuador; and Garuda Indonesia's former chief was jailed for bribes tied to Rolls-Royce and Airbus purchases.
implications: When a foreign-owned firm controls a chip plant or a strategic harbour, a quarrel between governments can stop supplies overnight, as European car workers found when Nexperia's chips stopped coming. Years of engineering work at TSMC or Samsung can leave with a few employees and come back as a competing factory. At state companies such as Eskom, Pemex or Garuda, a bribe means the contract went to the bidder who paid, and the public company and its customers carry the cost. Watch foreign purchases of chipmakers, ports and telecom suppliers, engineers moving between rival firms, and contract awards at state utilities and airlines.
uncertain: Huawei's trial and the Samsung case are charges, not verdicts, and Fujian Jinhua, the Chinese firm in the Micron case, was acquitted. A 2021 review found no security grounds to cancel the Darwin lease; the concern rests on the owner's Party ties, not on any finding of misuse.

title: Spyware and elections for hire
summary:
Elections in parts of Africa have become work for hire, with foreign firms selling campaign data, fake online accounts and hacking, and the same tools turn up against heads of government in Europe and North Africa. Most of these firms have closed or been blacklisted, but the methods are still sold. Cambridge Analytica, a British data firm, said on undercover film in 2018 that it ran Uhuru Kenyatta's 2013 and 2017 campaigns, surveyed 47,000 Kenyans and wrote the party's manifesto. Leaked emails show it worked with an Israeli outfit, Team Jorge, in Nigeria's 2015 election to discredit Muhammadu Buhari, who won anyway. Team Jorge's leader, filmed by reporters in 2023, claimed work on 33 presidential elections and showed access to the Telegram account of William Ruto's digital strategist in Kenya's 2022 race. Another Israeli firm, Archimedes Group, spent about $1.1 million on Facebook ads aimed at African elections before it was removed in 2019.

Russia's version ran through Yevgeny Prigozhin's political strategists. In Madagascar's 2018 presidential race, 15 to 20 of them dealt with as many as eight candidates, including the winner. In 2019 Facebook removed almost 200 fake accounts tied to him, with over a million followers, aimed at Madagascar, Mozambique, Congo, Sudan, Libya and three other African states.

Spyware sits beside this trade. NSO Group, an Israeli company, sells its Pegasus phone-hacking tool only to governments. A 2021 journalists' consortium reported that Morocco had selected more than 6,000 Algerian phones, including politicians and senior officers, and linked Morocco to President Macron's number; Morocco denies it. In Spain, the government said the prime minister's and defence minister's phones were infected in 2021 by someone it had not authorised. A US judge has found NSO liable for using WhatsApp's servers to reach about 1,400 users in 20 countries, and the US put NSO on a trade blacklist.
implications: Voters in Kenya, Nigeria, Madagascar or Zimbabwe usually never see these firms: the posts look local, the observers look independent and the data work hides behind a branding contract. The candidates who can pay gain, and the foreign firms or states that did the work then hold their secrets. Spyware sold to one government can be pointed at another country's leaders, as Algeria said of Morocco when it cut ties in 2021. Watch for unexplained consulting payments in campaign spending, bursts of new accounts before a vote, and observer missions nobody has heard of.
uncertain: Morocco denies being the Pegasus client behind the Algerian and French selections, and no one has been named for the Spanish infections; the Spanish High Court shelved its inquiry. Team Jorge's claim of 33 elections is its own sales pitch, filmed by reporters.

title: Scam compounds and casino money inside Asian states
summary:
In Cambodia and the Philippines today, scam compounds and offshore gambling firms have reached into government, and both countries are now prosecuting or shutting them. In the Philippines the vehicle was POGOs, Chinese-run online gambling firms licensed by the state gaming regulator from 2016 to serve players in China. They grew under President Rodrigo Duterte, and Senate hearings in 2024 tied many to fraud, human trafficking and torture. Alice Guo, elected mayor of Bamban in Tarlac in 2022, was linked to a raided hub, ruled a Chinese citizen and, in November 2025, sentenced to life for trafficking. Harry Roque, once Duterte's spokesman, faces arrest warrants with 49 others over a hub in Pampanga; he denies wrongdoing and has sought asylum in the Netherlands. President Marcos ordered all POGOs closed by the end of 2024, and Congress wrote the ban into law in October 2025.

In Cambodia the money sat closer to the top. Chen Zhi, born in China's Fujian province, became a Cambodian citizen in 2014, built the Prince Group into one of the country's largest conglomerates and advised Hun Sen, the interior minister and the head of the National Assembly. In October 2025 the US Justice Department indicted him as head of a cyber-fraud empire run from scam compounds and seized about 127,271 bitcoin, worth about $14 billion; in January 2026 Cambodia said it had arrested him and sent him to China. Huione Group, a Phnom Penh firm whose payment arm has Prime Minister Hun Manet's cousin Hun To as a director, lost its banking licence in March 2025 after the US Treasury found it had laundered more than $4 billion, including money from North Korean hackers.

What the compounds get is a licence, local officials who look away and a bank to move the money. It came out through Senate hearings and US prosecutions.
implications: The people who pay are the workers trafficked into compounds, held and made to defraud strangers, and the victims abroad who lose their savings. Nearby residents may see only a new walled site or a generous local donor, and when the owner advises national leaders or a leader's relative sits on the payment firm's board, police and regulators have little reason to look. Watch whether the Philippine ban holds or the business moves elsewhere, how Chen Zhi's case proceeds in China, and whether any Cambodian official tied to him or to Huione is investigated at home.
uncertain: Chen Zhi's US indictment has not been tried, and Roque denies the charges against him. No Cambodian official has been charged at home over links to Prince Group or Huione.

title: Iran's armed allies inside governments
roles: Where they sit in the state
summary:
In Lebanon and Iraq, armed groups backed by Iran hold ministries, seats and state-paid brigades in the open. In Lebanon, Hezbollah, a Shia party with its own armed wing, holds about 14 of 128 seats in parliament, and its picks run the health and labour ministries in the government formed in February 2025; with its ally Amal it controls six of 24 portfolios. At least 28 countries, including the US and UK, list it as a terrorist group. In August 2025 the cabinet approved the aim that only the state should hold weapons, and Hezbollah- and Amal-aligned ministers walked out; the army's disarmament plan has no timeline, and Hezbollah's leader Naim Qassem rejects it.

In Iraq the route was a law. The Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), about 67 mostly Shia factions formed in 2014 to fight Islamic State and almost all backed by Iran's Revolutionary Guards, became part of the armed forces in 2016, under the prime minister and paid from the state budget. Kata'ib Hezbollah, on the US terrorist list since 2009, staffs three of its brigades. The PMF chief of staff said in 2024 that it took orders from Iran's supreme leader, and its chairman, sanctioned by the US over the killing of protesters, remains in place.

In Syria, until Assad fell in December 2024, officers of the Quds Force, the Revolutionary Guards' foreign branch, were reported to command some 131 garrisons. Further away it works through money: in Gambia a businessman the US calls a key Hezbollah financier was among those holding monopolies under President Yahya Jammeh, OCCRP reported, and in 2023 the US sanctioned Paraguay's former president and sitting vice-president, citing ties to Hezbollah members. Kenya jailed two Iranians said to be Quds Force over explosives in 2013.

Iran gets a hand in war and security decisions in two capitals. The record comes from cabinet line-ups, laws, commanders' own statements and US sanctions.
implications: People in Lebanon and Iraq pay taxes that fund forces which, by their own commanders' statements, answer partly to Tehran, and decisions on war can be taken outside cabinet. In Lebanon the ministers running health and labour services are chosen by a party that keeps its own army. In Iraq the man the US sanctioned over the killing of protesters in 2019 still chairs the body that runs the PMF. Watch whether Lebanon's disarmament plan gets a timeline, whether Iraq passes the 2025 bill to tighten state control over the PMF, and who controls the ministries that hand out jobs and services.
uncertain: US sanctions are one government's judgement, not a court finding, and the US lifted its sanctions on Paraguay's Horacio Cartes in 2025. The figures on Iranian garrisons and bases in Syria are press reports.

title: Private forums where officials meet money
summary:
Many of the people running Western governments today also belong to a small set of private forums. The Bilderberg Meeting, a yearly off-the-record conference of about 130 politicians, executives and academics, met in Stockholm in June 2025 with Greece's prime minister, Finland's president, NATO's secretary general, five European Commissioners and two US regional military commanders on its list; Sweden's prime minister came without being listed. The World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders programme, which picks about 100 people under 40 a year, has taken sitting leaders into its classes: the prime ministers of Thailand and Montenegro in 2025 and of Ireland in 2018, along with ministers from Angola, India, the Netherlands and South Africa.

In the United States some forums write the policy as well as host the talk. The American Legislative Exchange Council (ALEC) has state legislators and corporate members draft 'model bills' together; about 1,000 bills based on them were being introduced each year when 850 models were published in 2011. The Federalist Society, a network of about 70,000 conservative lawyers, counted 43 of Trump's first 51 appeals-court nominees as members, and in 2025 Trump called it his 'recommending source' on judges. Authors of the Heritage Foundation's Project 2025 plan now hold posts such as budget director and FCC chair. Under Biden, nearly 70 staff from the Democratic-leaning Center for American Progress moved into his administration.

Elsewhere, free-market networks hold a similar place. Argentina's president Javier Milei won a prize from an Atlas Network partner, and members of the Mont Pelerin Society, an economists' society, have run finance ministries in New Zealand, Britain and Czechoslovakia and led Sri Lanka. The pattern is a century old: the Council on Foreign Relations wrote 682 confidential memos for the State Department during the Second World War, and Trilateral Commission members filled Jimmy Carter's cabinet.
uncertain: No forum in this record has been shown to direct a member's decisions; membership and office are documented, and the influence is inferred. Some attendance comes from news reports rather than official lists, such as Sweden's prime minister at Bilderberg 2025.

confirmed_by.title: Christian Science Monitor, 1980, on Trilateral Commission members in the Carter administration
ALEC Exposed (Center for Media and Democracy), 2011

implications: Membership is usually public and lawful; what stays private is what gets said. Officials who regulate banks, sign defence deals or pick judges spend days off the record with executives, and the same circle meets again under the next government, while opposition parties and small businesses have no seat. In the United States the effect is more direct: a bill in a statehouse may arrive already written at an ALEC meeting, and a federal judge may come off a society's list. Watch which ministers attend each year's Bilderberg, whether a bill in your state matches an ALEC model, and who drafted the plan a new administration follows.

title: Inside the international bodies

timeline.event: IOC expels ten members and sanctions ten over Salt Lake City bid gifts
Zeltner Committee report on tobacco-company efforts to undermine WHO
Salt Lake bid leaders Tom Welch and Dave Johnson acquitted of all federal charges
Council of Europe Assembly criticises WHO H1N1 decisions for lack of transparency on industry ties
Garcia report on 2018/2022 World Cup bids delivered; FIFA's summary clears Russia and Qatar; Garcia resigns

Ex-governor Sérgio Cabral testifies he paid $2 million for Rio Olympic votes

Meng Hongwei sentenced to 13.5 years for bribery

summary:
The bodies meant to stand above any one government or industry are dealing with outsiders inside them right now, and the European Union's institutions in Brussels are the busiest place. In the European Parliament, Belgian prosecutors say Qatar and Morocco paid members through a human-rights NGO; police seized about €1.5 million in cash in 2022, a vice-president was charged, and an appeal court let the case go ahead in 2026. In a second case, prosecutors allege associates of a former Huawei lobbyist paid MEPs from Italy, Bulgaria and Malta to sign a letter against curbs on foreign 5G equipment, and Parliament lifted one Italian member's immunity in June 2026. The Commission president's text messages with Pfizer's chief over the EU's largest vaccine contract were never released.

The same pull runs through the bodies for policing, food, health and money. Interpol, which police forces use to send wanted-person alerts, was led until 2025 by a senior UAE interior ministry officer after the UAE gave about $54 million; his Chinese predecessor vanished on a trip home and was jailed. A former Chinese vice-minister heads the UN food agency in Rome. The Gates Foundation was the WHO's second-largest funder in 2020, mostly for programmes it chooses. Reporters found Israeli intelligence spied on staff of the International Criminal Court in The Hague. At the climate summits, the UAE's 2023 president ran its state oil company and Azerbaijan's 2024 chief executive was filmed discussing gas deals.

Sport shows how deep it goes once proven. A US indictment says FIFA voters from Trinidad and Tobago, Guatemala, Brazil and Paraguay were paid to back Russia and Qatar as World Cup hosts, a Paris court convicted the head of world athletics of selling doping cover-ups to Russia. In Guatemala, the president shut the UN-backed anti-impunity commission in 2019 while it was investigating his campaign.
uncertain: The Qatargate and Huawei defendants deny wrongdoing and have not been tried; Al-Raisi denies the torture allegations, and Israel denies the ICC spying. Attending Bilderberg, as NATO's chief and five Commissioners did in 2025, is lawful and is not evidence of wrongdoing.

confirmed_by.title: WHO Committee of Experts on Tobacco Industry Documents, Tobacco Company Strategies to Undermine Tobacco Control Activities at the World Health Organization, July 2000
US v. Webb et al. (FIFA), E.D.N.Y.

implications: These bodies decide things that reach ordinary people across borders: whose name goes out on a police alert, which health programmes get money, how climate deals are worded and which countries host sporting events. A person can be arrested abroad on another state's request, as a refugee footballer was in Bangkok in 2018 on a Bahraini notice Interpol later withdrew. In Guatemala, cases the UN commission had built lost their investigators. Watch large voluntary gifts before votes for top posts, officials moving between a body and their own government, immunity votes in the European Parliament, and the oil and gas ties of each climate summit's hosts.

title: Movements that sought the state itself

countries.note: A military court convicted Brigadier Ali Khan and four majors in 2012 of links to Hizb ut-Tahrir.
The army said in January 2012 it had stopped a coup by serving and retired officers linked to Hizb ut-Tahrir.

summary:
Today the Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt in 1928 with branches across the Arab world, is being pushed out of governments it once helped run. Unlike most groups on this map it usually stood openly for election, and won. In Egypt, Mohamed Morsi became president in 2012 and the army removed him in 2013; the Brotherhood has been banned there since. In Jordan its party, the Islamic Action Front, won 31 of 138 seats in 2024 and is the largest in parliament, yet the government banned the movement itself in April 2025. In Tunisia, Ennahda, which comes from the Brotherhood tradition but denies any organisational tie, led the government from 2011 to 2014; its leader Rached Ghannouchi, a former speaker of parliament, is now in prison with further sentences of 22 and 14 years handed down in 2025, which his party calls political. Morocco's Brotherhood-inspired PJD led the government for ten years before losing 113 seats in 2021. In Kuwait its offshoot Hadas regularly won seats in the 1990s and 2000s.

Sudan is where the tradition held the state longest: the Brotherhood-derived National Islamic Front helped Omar al-Bashir take power in 1989, and in 2025 the US sanctioned the finance minister and an Islamist militia fighting beside the army. In January 2026 the US listed the Egyptian, Jordanian and Lebanese branches as terrorists. Saudi Arabia and the UAE had already done so in 2014, and the UAE jailed 56 people, many from the Islah group, in 2013 for plotting to seize power.

The second movement, Hizb ut-Tahrir, founded in 1953, calls for one worldwide caliphate and does not run for office; it tries to recruit officers instead. Pakistan's army convicted a brigadier and four majors over it in 2012, Bangladesh's army named it in a foiled coup plot that year, and Indonesia (2017) and Britain (2024) banned it.
uncertain: Ennahda and Morocco's PJD deny being Brotherhood branches, and Tunisia's prosecutions of Ennahda leaders are disputed as political. Sudan's 2021 court ruling overturned dismissals of Bashir-era judges and prosecutors, so how far Islamists still hold the judiciary is unclear.

confirmed_by.title: Egyptian cabinet designation, 25 December 2013
Pakistan Army field general court martial, August 2012

implications: Here the question is less who hides inside a government than who is allowed into it. When Brotherhood parties won votes their people took office openly; opponents later called them infiltrators and removed them, in Egypt by a coup. For voters in Jordan, the largest party they elected now sits beside a parent movement that is banned. The label is also stretched: Austria's 2020 raids on suspected Brotherhood networks were ruled unlawful, and a 2025 French report on 'entryism' in local councils found no recent document showing a plan for an Islamic state in France. Watch what happens to the Islamic Action Front's seats, and whether other governments follow the US designations.

title: Lodges inside police forces and courts
summary:
In Britain, Italy and Romania the live question is whether police, judges and ministers belong to lodges the public cannot see. Freemasonry is a lawful private fraternity, and belonging to it is not wrongdoing. But police and judges are meant to owe loyalty only to the law, and a person arrested or tried cannot tell whether the officer or judge shares a private oath with the other side.

London's Metropolitan Police has required officers and staff to declare Freemasonry since December 2025; 397 had done so by February 2026, and the High Court refused the United Grand Lodge of England's bid to stop the rule, calling it proportionate. Britain has argued about this since the 1980s, when a Leicester shop owner and his son, assaulted at a ladies' night of a Blackburn lodge made up mostly of officers, were themselves charged, then acquitted. New judges and police had to declare from 1998; for judges the rule was dropped in 2009, after a review found 5.4% were masons and no evidence of impropriety. In Romania a magazine reported in 2019 that the interim interior minister and the Gendarmerie chief were masons.

Italy shows what a secret lodge inside the state can do. The 1981 list of Propaganda Due (P2), a lodge run by Licio Gelli, named the heads of all three intelligence services and 195 military officers; in 2025 Italy's top court made final a verdict calling Gelli the knowing financier of the 1980 Bologna station bombing. A 1982 law banning secret societies that interfere with public bodies was used in 2018 against the 'P3' network, in which a former head of Italy's top court was convicted of abuse of office. Elsewhere, Cuba's former Grand Master admitted in 2011 that he worked for state security, and in 1920s Denver a Klansman mayor made a Klansman police chief.

It came out through police searches, parliamentary inquiries and trials.
uncertain: A membership list shows who joined, not what anyone did for the lodge. The Romanian report rests on press accounts, and Gelli and others were acquitted in 1994–96 of conspiracy against the state through P2.

confirmed_by.title: House of Commons Home Affairs Committee, Freemasonry in the Police and the Judiciary, 1997; Freemasonry in Public Life, 1999
Italian Parliamentary Anti-Mafia Commission, report on Freemasonry, December 2017

implications: For someone facing the police or the courts, the risk is a hidden loyalty they cannot check, even when none is in play. Britain's parliament said it got the Grand Lodge's cooperation only 'through compulsion', and the Grand Lodge needed five attempts to produce a list of masons in one disbanded West Midlands detective squad. Italy learned who sat in P2 only because a search for something else found the list. Britain is moving toward disclosure for police and away from it for judges. Watch whether other police forces follow the Met, and how undeclared memberships are handled, such as the Romanian ministers named in 2019.

title: French lodges and African presidencies
roles: Head of state or minister in a lodge
case_role: Head of state or minister in a lodge

countries.note: The Grande Loge Nationale Française and the Grand Orient de France sponsored or chartered lodges in former colonies; the GLNF's grand master installed Ali Bongo as grand master of Gabon's lodge in 2009. Jacques Foccart's Service d'Action Civique ran France's African networks from the Élysée.

summary:
In several former French colonies in Central and West Africa, Masonic lodges linked to Paris still sit close to the presidency. In the Republic of Congo, President Denis Sassou-Nguesso is reported to be grand master of the national lodge tied to the Grande Loge Nationale Française (GLNF), a French Masonic body, and the Central African Republic's former president François Bozizé reportedly joined under his sponsorship. In Gabon the grand mastership traditionally went with the presidency. Omar Bongo, president from 1967 to 2009, founded two lodges, one linked to the GLNF and one to the Grand Orient de France, France's largest Masonic body, and in 2009 the GLNF's grand master installed his son Ali in the post the year Ali became president. After the 2023 coup removed Ali, the lodge passed to a provincial governor, and the head of the Grand Orient reportedly met the coup leader, Brice Oligui Nguema, in secret and offered support; Oligui was elected president in 2025.

A 2012 Jeune Afrique survey traced the same pattern across the region. Burkina Faso's president Blaise Compaoré was a former grand master succeeded by his foreign minister; the presidents of Mali and Guinea oversaw national lodges; Senegal's Abdoulaye Wade had been initiated; Côte d'Ivoire's prime minister and interior minister were members; and Gabon's police chief led one lodge. Chad's Idriss Déby and Niger's Mamadou Tandja were also named. Le Monde reported in 1999 that Cameroon's Paul Biya gave tens of millions of francs to a French Templar order, OSTI, with money moving from the state oil company to its founder. Liberia, never a French colony, shows the same habit: by the 1970s most high officials were Masons and the president was grand master.

The French side has its own history, from a War Ministry that sorted army officers for promotion using Grand Orient files around 1904, to the Gaullist militia SAC, co-founded by de Gaulle's Africa adviser Jacques Foccart.
uncertain: Most memberships here come from press reports, chiefly Jeune Afrique, not from lodge records, and some were denied, as Macky Sall denied membership in Senegal. Nothing in this record shows a lodge directing a state decision; it shows who sat in the same room.

confirmed_by.title: Jeune Afrique, investigation of Freemasonry in Africa, 2012
Le Monde, 1999, on payments to the Ordre Souverain du Temple Initiatique

implications: Lodges are lawful, and membership is not wrongdoing. What the record shows is a private room where African presidents, ministers and police chiefs meet French Masonic leaders, out of view of parliaments in Paris and citizens in Libreville and Brazzaville. A Gabonese citizen could not easily know that the president and the police chief both led lodges sponsored from France, and several of these presidents ruled for decades. Watch who meets new leaders after a coup or election, whether grand masterships still pass with the presidency, and whether any lodge publishes its officers.

title: Banks and banking families
summary:
Banks reach governments today mostly through the people who move between them. Canada's prime minister since March 2025, Mark Carney, spent 13 years at Goldman Sachs before running the central banks of Canada and England. Germany's chancellor Friedrich Merz chaired the German arm of BlackRock, the world's largest asset manager. In Argentina, two former JPMorgan bankers have run the economy ministry and the central bank since December 2023. Central bank governors from 60-plus jurisdictions meet every two months in Basel at the Bank for International Settlements, the central banks' own bank, whose committee writes the world's bank rules.

In other places banks and the state are owned by the same circle. In Lebanon, a 2016 study found 18 of 20 major banks had shareholders tied to the political class; the system collapsed in 2019. In Russia, the US Treasury called Bank Rossiya, founded by friends of Vladimir Putin, the personal bank for senior officials. In Sweden, the Wallenberg family's foundations control companies worth about 35% of the Stockholm market through voting shares. In Ukraine, the state had to bail out PrivatBank for $5.6 billion after loans to firms of its co-owner, a former regional governor.

Banks also arrange the debts governments hide. Goldman's swaps hid about €2.8 billion of Greek debt as Greece entered the euro; Credit Suisse and Russia's VTB lent Mozambican state companies over $1 billion behind parliament's back; Goldman bankers arranged the bond deals of Malaysia's 1MDB fund. The roots go back to 1803, when Barings financed the Louisiana Purchase, and to 1910, when bankers met on Jekyll Island to draft the Federal Reserve plan. Claims that Jewish banking families such as the Rothschilds secretly own the Fed or control the world's wars are antisemitic conspiracy theories; the Fed's board is appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate.
implications: When a banker becomes finance minister or central bank governor, or a bank is hired to manage public money or debt talks, the public rarely sees whose interests are weighed. In Lebanon, depositors lost savings to banks owned by the people who wrote the rules. In Greece and Mozambique, people later paid for debts they had not been told about. In Afghanistan, Kabul Bank paid soldiers' and police salaries while about $900 million went to insiders. Watch who is named to run finance ministries and central banks, which banks advise on debt and privatisation, what the Basel meetings agree, and treat any account that blames a Jewish family for all of it as having left the record.
uncertain: Moving between banks and government is usually legal and public, and most of the people named here have not been accused of wrongdoing. Najib Razak is appealing his 1MDB conviction, and the Fed is not secretly owned by any banking family: its board is appointed and confirmed in public.

title: Rhodes, Milner and the Round Table network

countries.note: Rhodes's trustees, Milner, the Round Table journal (from 1910), Chatham House (1920) and the Pilgrims Society's London branch. Members held the posts of War Cabinet minister (Milner, 1916–18), the prime minister's private secretary (Philip Kerr, 1916–21) and editor of The Times (Geoffrey Dawson, 1912–19 and 1923–41).

Milner was High Commissioner from 1897. After 1902 his young staff ran the Transvaal and Orange River Colony administrations and worked for the 1910 Union. Patrick Duncan, one of them, became Governor-General in 1937.
Round Table group from 1909; Earl Grey, a Rhodes trustee, was Governor General 1904–11.
Round Table group from 1910; Quigley names Australia and Canada as the first dominion institutes of international affairs (1927).
Round Table group from 1910.

The Council on Foreign Relations, founded in 1921 after the 1919 Hotel Majestic agreement in Paris, and the Pilgrims Society's New York branch (1903). The CFR's War and Peace Studies project sent memoranda to the State Department from 1939 to 1945.

summary:
This is where one of today's habits comes from: drawing the people who run foreign policy from a small set of colleges, clubs and research institutes. It started in southern Africa. Cecil Rhodes, premier of the Cape Colony, left his fortune to extend British rule, and lost office in 1896 over the Jameson Raid, a failed armed incursion into the Boer Transvaal. Alfred Milner, High Commissioner there from 1897, recruited young Oxford graduates, his 'Kindergarten', to run the conquered Transvaal; they pressed for the 1910 Union of South Africa and founded the Round Table movement, with a journal and groups in Canada, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa.

The same circle then filled offices across the empire. In London, Milner sat in Lloyd George's five-man War Cabinet from 1916, the Round Table's first editor became the prime minister's private secretary, and Milner's former secretary edited The Times through the 1930s, writing in 1937 that he cut anything that might hurt German opinion. Two Rhodes trustees or Kindergarten members became governors-general of Canada, one became governor-general of South Africa, and Quigley credits a Round Table study group with the 1919 design of India's provincial government.

At the 1919 Paris peace conference, British and American experts agreed to found Chatham House in London and the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR) in New York. From 1939 the CFR ran confidential post-war planning for the State Department, paid for by the Rockefeller Foundation; Allen Dulles led one of its groups and later ran the CIA, and a 1977 study found more than half of 502 senior US officials of 1945 to 1972 were members. The historian Carroll Quigley described a secret society behind all this, founded around Rhodes in 1891, but that inner society rests on his account alone. Chatham House and the CFR remain leading foreign-policy institutes, and the Pilgrims Society still welcomes each new US ambassador in London.
uncertain: Quigley's secret 'Society of the Elect' rests on his reading of papers others have not published, and which officials belonged to it is his attribution. From 1970 writers such as W. Cleon Skousen recast his account as a world conspiracy of international bankers, a reading Quigley rejected and the record does not support.

confirmed_by.title: Carroll Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment (written 1949, published 1981)
Carroll Quigley, Tragedy and Hope (1966)
Council on Foreign Relations, centennial history (2021)

implications: Nearly everyone here held office openly and was appointed through normal channels; the record shows how few doors those channels had. For about half a century a few hundred people from the same Oxford colleges, South African administration and London and New York clubs supplied private secretaries, editors, governors and planners on both sides of the Atlantic, so voters chose a party while the briefings its ministers read were drafted inside the circle. The practical lesson today is to look past who wins an election to who staffs the offices, writes the briefings and funds the think tanks.
