title: The anticommunist web, 1945–1990

countries.note: Gladio, disclosed by Prime Minister Andreotti on 24 October 1990, and P2, whose 1981 list held the heads of all three intelligence services. Italy is where the stay-behind and lodge networks overlapped most.
The Chilean intelligence service DINA under Manuel Contreras called the founding meeting of Operation Condor in Santiago in November 1975.
CIA support for the stay-behind networks is confirmed in the Italian and Belgian inquiries; Condor's 1976 bombing of Orlando Letelier in Washington was carried out by DINA agents.

summary:
Much of what this map shows today traces back to a web of secret armies, lodges and intelligence clubs built across Western Europe, Latin America and the Middle East during the Cold War to fight communism. After the Second World War NATO, the Western military alliance, coordinated 'stay-behind' networks of officers and civilians with hidden weapons caches, meant to resist a Soviet invasion. Italy's was called Gladio. When the prime minister disclosed it in 1990, Belgium, Switzerland, Greece, Germany and the Netherlands admitted or investigated their own. Switzerland's P-26 spent 54.3 million francs outside parliament's control, and the full report on it stays sealed until 2041.

In Italy the P2 lodge listed 962 names in 1981, among them two sitting ministers and the heads of all three intelligence services; in Argentina its members included a junta admiral and a social welfare minister whose ministry funded the Triple A death squad. In Greece a secret officers' society, IDEA, supplied leaders of the 1967 coup. In Turkey a 1996 car crash near Susurluk put an Istanbul deputy police chief, an MP and a Grey Wolves leader in one car. From 1975 the secret police of six South American dictatorships hunted opponents across borders as Operation Condor, and killed a former Chilean foreign minister in Washington. In 1976 the intelligence chiefs of France, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Iran and Morocco formed the 'Safari Club'.

Most of this came to light through a change of government, a parliamentary inquiry or files found by chance, such as Condor's records in a Paraguayan police station in 1992. Files are still being opened and courts are still ruling: a Rome appeals court gave 24 life sentences in the Condor case in 2019, and in 2025 Italy's top court confirmed a verdict calling P2's head the knowing financier of the 1980 Bologna station bombing, which killed 85 people.
uncertain: Gelli and others were acquitted of conspiracy against the state through P2, and the P2 list shows membership, not what each member did. The full Swiss P-26 report stays sealed until 2041, so what it says is not known.

confirmed_by.title: European Parliament resolution on Gladio, 22 November 1990
Belgian Senate parliamentary inquiry on stay-behind networks, 1991
US National Security Archive, Operation Condor briefing books

implications: These networks were built for an invasion that never came, and their people, weapons and secrecy were turned on opponents at home. Condor's victims were exiles and dissidents. In Italy, P2 members headed the intelligence services during years of bombings, and Gelli and a P2-listed intelligence general were convicted over a suitcase of explosives planted to send the Bologna inquiry the wrong way. In Argentina, Chile, Uruguay and Italy, victims' cases reached verdicts thirty to forty years later. Bodies set up in secret for an emergency outlasted it, and parliaments learned of them last. Watch for sealed records such as Switzerland's P-26 report, and for courts still ruling on the 1970s and 1980s.

summary:
This is where today's ways of moving money quietly for powerful clients come from: in the 1970s and 1980s a few banks grew because governments, a church and intelligence services needed money moved without questions. Through Italy, the Vatican and the offshore centres of Luxembourg, Nassau and Panama, the network ran through Banco Ambrosiano, Milan's largest private bank. Its chairman, Roberto Calvi, belonged to P2, a secret Masonic lodge whose seized list held 962 names, including the heads of all three Italian intelligence services, and its main shareholder was the Vatican Bank (IOR), the Holy See's own bank. When about $1.3 billion went missing in 1982, Calvi was found hanged under a London bridge. The Vatican Bank denied liability but paid creditors $224 million, and Italy's top court ruled that the 1929 treaty with the Vatican shielded its president from arrest. Ambrosiano's units in Lima and Managua reached into Peru's arms purchases and Nicaragua's politics.

BCCI, the Bank of Credit and Commerce International, ran a second network out of Abu Dhabi, whose government and ruling family owned 77% of it by 1991, across Latin America, the Caribbean and the United States. A US Senate inquiry found it secretly owned Washington's largest bank, held about $25 million for Panama's General Manuel Noriega, handled most of Jamaica's government foreign-currency accounts and held deposits from the central banks of Peru and Paraguay; a former Saudi intelligence chief fronted its US takeover. The CIA kept using it after it knew the bank was criminal. Regulators shut BCCI in 1991. In Sydney, Nugan Hand Bank, whose staff included retired US generals and admirals, collapsed in 1980.

The thread runs into the present at the Vatican, whose court convicted a former Vatican Bank president of embezzlement in 2021; its 2023 conviction of Cardinal Angelo Becciu over a London property was annulled in 2026, with a retrial ordered.
uncertain: Calvi's death was first ruled suicide and then left open; a 2002 forensic report for an Italian court concluded he was murdered. Clark Clifford's charges were dropped on health grounds and his partner Robert Altman was acquitted, so the Senate's findings about them were never tested to a verdict, and Nugan Hand's intelligence links rest on who worked there.

confirmed_by.title: US Senate, The BCCI Affair (Kerry–Brown report), 1992
Bank of Italy inquiry into Banco Ambrosiano, 1981–82
Royal Commission of Inquiry into Drug Trafficking (Stewart), 1983–85

implications: Each of these banks was licensed and supervised, and the warnings came years early: the Bank of Italy flagged Ambrosiano in 1978, and US agencies had information on BCCI's hidden ownership from 1981. They stayed open because their customers included a church, spy services, a dictator and an oil state. When they fell, depositors and creditor banks lost money, and whole countries carried the risk: Peru's central bank had $270 million, about three-tenths of its cash reserves, at BCCI-Panama in 1987. The officials who used them were rarely convicted. Watch for banks whose clients are governments; they are the slowest to be closed.

title: Sworn brotherhoods that chose who governed

countries.note: Every prime minister and state president from D. F. Malan (1948) to F. W. de Klerk (1989–94) was a member of the Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret Afrikaner men's society founded in 1918. Its membership list was published by journalists Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom in 1978.

Army officers who later founded the Black Hand killed King Alexander Obrenović in 1903 and its leader, Colonel Dragutin Dimitrijević 'Apis', became head of military intelligence; its rival, the White Hand, put General Petar Živković in power as prime minister in 1929.
IDEA, a secret society of army officers, prepared the April 1967 coup; the colonels ruled until 1974 and were tried in 1975.

The Society of St. Tammany ran New York City's Democratic machine; the Know Nothings won Massachusetts in 1854; the 1920s Klan elected governors in Indiana, Colorado and Oregon and helped send Hugo Black to the Senate and then the Supreme Court.

summary:
This is where today's arrangements come from: in some countries a sworn society did not slip into the government, it chose who formed one. In South Africa the Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret all-male Afrikaner society founded in 1918, counted every prime minister and state president from 1948 to 1994 as members, from D. F. Malan to F. W. de Klerk. A 1979 report put it at about 12,000 members in 800 cells and said all but two cabinet ministers belonged; the army chief and the head of the security service were members, and its own chairman became education minister in 1980.

In the Balkans the societies were made of army officers. Serbian officers who killed their king in 1903 founded the Black Hand in 1911, and its leader became chief of military intelligence; a rival White Hand officer became Yugoslavia's prime minister in 1929. In Greece, IDEA, a secret society of officers who had served in wartime collaborationist battalions, supplied several leaders of the 1967 coup, who ruled until 1974 and were convicted of high treason in 1975.

In North America and Ireland, lodges built political machines. Orangemen, members of a Protestant fraternal order, held Toronto's mayoralty for about a century until 1954, and four Canadian prime ministers belonged. The Tammany Society ran New York City under 'Boss' Tweed, and in 1854 the secret Know Nothing order took the Massachusetts governorship and almost the whole legislature. In the 1920s the Ku Klux Klan put governors in Indiana, Colorado and Alabama and a mayor in Denver, who made a Klansman police chief. Irish ministers in 1948 belonged to the Catholic Knights of Saint Columbanus. The thread reaches the present: in 2014 an FBI inquiry found a deputy police chief and an officer in Fruitland Park, Florida, had been involved with the Klan.
uncertain: Membership lists for most of these societies were secret and come from journalists, historians and later testimony, so individual memberships are often 'probable' rather than proven. The idea that Cecil Rhodes's society steered British policy through Alfred Milner is the historian Carroll Quigley's reading, not an established finding.

confirmed_by.title: Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom, The Super-Afrikaners (1978)
Greek junta trials, 1975
Indiana and Colorado Klan histories; Hugo Black's radio address, 1 October 1937

implications: Where one society picks the leaders, an election only decides which of its members holds the job. South Africans who were not white Afrikaner men had no route into the Broederbond, so for 46 years they had no route into the circle that chose their prime ministers, generals and broadcasters. The same thing happened on a smaller scale in Denver, where the mayor and police chief answered to the Klan, and in Toronto's city hall. Watch for the same sign today: one private body supplying the ministers, police chiefs and media heads at once.

title: Intelligence money behind international NGOs

countries.note: The CIA funded these bodies through foundations and pass-through grants; the Senate Church Committee (1976) found CIA money in at least 108 of 700 large grants made by 164 foundations in 1963–66. After 1983 the National Endowment for Democracy took over part of this work openly, with public money.

summary:
This is where today's quarrels over foreign-funded civic groups come from. In the early Cold War the CIA, the US foreign intelligence agency, quietly paid for a set of bodies that looked private and independent. From Paris, the Congress for Cultural Freedom, run by a CIA officer, Michael Josselson, had offices in 35 countries and more than 20 magazines, among them Encounter in London. From Munich, Radio Free Europe and Radio Liberty broadcast into the Soviet bloc on CIA money until 1971 to 1972. In Asia, the Asia Foundation, which began as the CIA-funded Committee for a Free Asia, was described in a 1966 CIA memo as 'a Central Intelligence Agency proprietary'. At home, the US National Student Association took CIA money until a former staffer exposed it in 1967, and in 1976 the Senate's Church Committee found CIA money in at least 108 of 700 large grants made by 164 US foundations in 1963 to 1966.

The same channels reached into other countries' elections and unions. The historian Anthony Carew found the CIA paid the American Federation of Labor's Free Trade Union Committee for about 20 years, starting with Italy's 1948 election. In Brazil the CIA-linked Brazilian Institute of Democratic Action paid for opposition candidates for Congress and eleven governorships in 1962, and a US labour institute's director later said its Brazilian trainees were 'intimately involved' in the 1964 coup.

From 1983 much of this work moved into the open through the National Endowment for Democracy (NED), funded by Congress; its founder said in 1991 that much of what it did had been done covertly by the CIA 25 years earlier. Its roughly $2 million in Nicaragua in 1984 to 1988 was the opposition's main open aid before the 1990 election. Today Russia (2015) and China (2019) cite this history when they ban or sanction the NED as a front.
uncertain: How far AIFLD trainees shaped Brazil's 1964 coup rests largely on its director's later statement. Russia's and China's claims that today's NED is an intelligence front are their governments' assertions; the NED is funded openly by Congress.

confirmed_by.title: US Senate Select Committee on Intelligence Activities (Church Committee), Final Report, Book I, 1976

implications: The people reading the magazines, joining the student federation and voting in Italy or Brazil thought they were dealing with independent groups; nobody told them a foreign intelligence service was paying, or that the same money backed particular parties. Funding of this kind is now mostly published, through the NED and others, but the old secret funding hands governments a ready reason to treat any foreign-funded group as suspect, and Russia and China use it to shut groups they dislike. For a reader, the useful questions about any civic group, magazine or broadcaster are who pays for it and whether that is disclosed.

title: Lenders, aid programmes and trained technocrats
roles: Country whose economy was run by the trainees or advisers

countries.note: The Ford Foundation paid for Indonesian economists to train at Berkeley; the US aid agency (ICA, later USAID) funded the 1956 agreement between the University of Chicago and Chile's Catholic University; the US Treasury ran the Saudi Joint Commission from a Saudi-funded trust account.

summary:
This is where one thread on today's map begins: a country's economy run by people trained or paid through another country's programmes, which continues now in the conditions lenders attach to loans. From the 1950s to the 1980s, in Indonesia, Chile and Saudi Arabia, US money helped put such people in charge of state spending.

In Indonesia, the Ford Foundation, a large US private foundation, paid in the late 1950s for University of Indonesia economists to take doctorates at the University of California, Berkeley. When Suharto took power in 1966 they became his economic team: Widjojo Nitisastro ran the planning agency BAPPENAS from 1967 to 1983, and Ali Wardhana was finance minister, the post that controls the state's money, from 1968 to 1983. Their programme cut inflation from 650% to 13% by 1969 and opened the country to foreign investors.

In Chile, a US aid scheme, later funded by the Ford Foundation, linked Santiago's Catholic University with the University of Chicago and trained 126 Chilean students by 1973. Their plan, 'El ladrillo' ('the brick'), became the junta's economic programme in 1975, and its graduates ran the economy and finance ministries until the 1982 debt crisis; one of them, Miguel Kast, became Central Bank governor that year.

In Saudi Arabia, a joint commission set up in 1974 and co-chaired by the US Treasury Secretary supplied US advisers paid from a Saudi account in the US Treasury; a 1979 US audit found it recycled oil money into US goods and services.

John Perkins, once chief economist at the Boston engineering firm Chas. T. Main, wrote in 2004 that his job was to inflate growth forecasts so countries such as Indonesia would take large loans for US-built projects; parts of his account are disputed. The loans of this era were left for later governments to repay, and the Loan Conditions map on this site follows that story through the lenders' own terms.
uncertain: The New York Times found Perkins's career described accurately but no evidence that the National Security Agency recruited him, and the State Department called much of his account fabricated. That foreign training made these ministers serve US interests, rather than their own convictions, is an argument, not a finding.

confirmed_by.title: US General Accounting Office report on the US–Saudi Arabian Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation, 1979
New York Times, 'Economic Hit Man' review, 2005

implications: No secret oath is needed when a country's economic ministries are staffed by people trained, paid or advised through another country's institutions. The choices those ministers made, such as privatisation, opening to foreign capital and borrowing for large projects, shaped the lives of millions who never voted for them; in Indonesia and Chile they served military governments, and later governments carried the debts. For a reader today, the things to look for are who trained a country's finance and central-bank officials, who pays its foreign advisers, and which outside lenders set conditions on its budget.

summary:
This is where the usual shape of today's infiltration stories comes from: across the record, a network is exposed, then banned or purged, and years later courts often narrow or undo the findings. Exposure tends to come by accident. In Italy in 1981, financial police searching a factory in a case about another banker found the list of the secret P2 lodge, 962 names including the heads of all three intelligence services, and their own commander phoned to say he was on it. In Turkey a 1996 car crash at Susurluk put an MP, a police chief and a wanted Grey Wolves gunman in one car. Italy and Switzerland learned of hidden Cold War networks, Gladio and P-26, in 1990.

Purges follow, often under a law written for the purpose, and the map records them in 73 countries. Egypt declared the Muslim Brotherhood terrorist in 2013, and Jordan banned it in 2025 although its party held the most seats in parliament. Turkey removed 2,745 judges the day after its 2016 coup attempt and took over 784 companies it linked to the Gülen movement. Japan's courts ordered the Unification Church dissolved after its ties to ruling-party lawmakers came out, and upheld the order in March 2026; the Philippines banned offshore gaming operators after a Senate inquiry. In 12 countries, from South Korea and Taiwan to Peru and Moldova, a parliament or commission did the exposing.

Reversals are recorded in 23 countries. Rome courts acquitted P2's leader and others of conspiracy in the 1990s. In Turkey all remaining Sledgehammer defendants were acquitted in 2015 once the evidence proved forged, and the Ergenekon convictions fell in 2016. Brazil's Supreme Court annulled Lula's Car Wash convictions, Panama acquitted the Mossack Fonseca founders in 2024, Sudan's courts overturned dismissals of Islamist-era judges, and the US lifted sanctions on Paraguay's former president.
uncertain: A reversal does not always mean the first finding was wrong: Sledgehammer's evidence was shown to be forged, while the Mossack Fonseca acquittal rested on evidence the judge called insufficient and improperly gathered.

implications: In Turkey, Egypt or Jordan, a purge reaches past proven members: anyone tied to the wrong school, company or association can lose a job, a business or a party. In Italy, Brazil or Panama, a later acquittal leaves people unsure which version to believe, and it can return real members to public life alongside those wrongly accused. Exposure rarely comes from the bodies meant to watch for it; it comes from a raid on something else, a crash, a leak or a change of government. With any new case on this map, ask which stage it is at, who exposed it and why then, and whether a court has tested it yet.
